title: Tell me about a time you influenced people without formal authority
prompt: Tell me about a time you tried to build agreement with people you could not direct. Explain their concerns, how you approached them, and what happened. The outcome can be agreement, a compromise, a reasoned refusal or an issue that remained open.
blurb: Influence without authority (senior): did they persuade with evidence, empathy and trust — or just escalate?

rubric.label: Situation & the ask
rubric.description: Explains the desired change, the people involved and why the candidate could not simply direct it.

rubric.label: Owning the outcome
rubric.description: Identifies their contribution to understanding the other parties’ needs and building a workable path without claiming authority they did not have.

rubric.label: Specific contribution and decisions
rubric.description: Describes a concrete influence method such as listening, evidence, a small trial, an alternative or a shared goal; justified escalation is allowed.

rubric.label: Outcome and evidence
rubric.description: Describes the actual response and consequences with supported qualitative or quantitative evidence; success does not require persuading everyone.

rubric.label: Reflection & relationships
rubric.description: Explains limits of persuasion, what could improve a future approach and when a boundary or escalation is appropriate.

rubric.label: Clear, relevant communication
rubric.description: Makes the relevant situation, reasoning and contribution understandable in any clear order. No required STAR structure, pronouns, performance of confidence or emotional tone.

reference.scenario: Explore an attempt to build agreement across different priorities without direct authority. A peer group, volunteer activity or professional setting is suitable. Assess the approach and understanding of concerns, not the power to obtain a yes or pressure someone past a legitimate boundary.
model_points: States a concrete change and why another person might reasonably view it differently.
Asks or otherwise checks the other party’s concerns rather than guessing their motives.
Uses a specific method, such as a demonstration, evidence, an alternative or a limited trial.
Respects consent, authority and legitimate limits; uses an appropriate escalation when the risk warrants it.
Describes agreement, compromise, refusal or uncertainty accurately and explains what was learned.
Reflects on relationships and future collaboration without making approval from others a prerequisite for a strong answer.

probes.trigger: candidate assumes the other party’s motives
probes.question: How did you learn what mattered to them?

probes.trigger: candidate says only that they persuaded someone
probes.question: What did you do that helped them consider the idea?

probes.trigger: candidate mentions escalation without its purpose
probes.question: What made escalation appropriate at that point?

red_flags: Uses knowingly false evidence, threats or deception to obtain agreement.
Claims voluntary agreement when their own account describes coercion.
Dismisses an explicitly stated safety or consent boundary as an obstacle to winning.
follow_ups: What would you try if the person still disagreed?
What did their response teach you about your proposal?
reference.exemplar_answer: Illustrative example only; it is not a required setting, answer order or achievement standard. Other volunteers disliked my idea for a shared handoff sheet because a previous form took too long. I asked which parts had been burdensome, then showed a version with only the next action and owner. Two people agreed to try it for a shift; another preferred the existing method. We compared what was missed and kept one useful field. I learned more from the objections than from trying to sell the full idea.
reference.assessment_contract: Assess the selected competency from concrete job-relevant evidence. Examples from paid work, study, volunteering, caregiving, informal work, military service and community activities are equally eligible when relevant. A modest example is sufficient if it shows the competency; employer prestige, formal title and financial scale are not criteria. Accept qualitative or quantitative outcomes supported by the account, including partial or unsuccessful outcomes. Do not require a numeric metric, STAR order, particular pronouns, composure, enthusiasm or a particular communication style. Identify personal contribution by meaning while preserving credit to others. Assess intelligibility and relevance, not accent, fluency, verbosity, visible emotion, disability or private circumstances. Mark genuinely missing evidence not assessed; do not infer poor competence or dishonesty from an absent example. A clearly labeled hypothetical may be discussed as situational practice but must not count as demonstrated past experience. Respect scope of practice, authorization, safety and ethical duties; pausing, declining, reporting or escalating can be sound judgment. Never require obedience, direct confrontation, unpaid overwork or successful persuasion regardless of the circumstances.
